subject: Basic question about the posterior distribution

messages.author: 12836e6a447153b7
messages.subject: Basic question about the posterior distribution
parts:
Hey all,
 
I am using the spde model to model a Gaussian field. Suppose the observations {y_obs} are assumed to be GF, and is approximated by \sum_{k=1}^m w_k\psi_k which is the finite element representation and is also the solution to the spde. Now I can make predictions on the other locations {s_prd} using R-inla to get the posterior predictive mean and sd of the {y_prd}. 
But I want to know what is the posterior predictive distribution of {y_prd | y_obs}? Since Gaussian likelihood is used, is that also Gaussian or at least can be approximated by a Gaussian? If so, what is the mean (posterior mean) and covariance structure?
 
Thanks a lot in adavance!
 
Best wishes,
Ming

> is also the solution to the spde. Now I can make predictions on the
> other locations {s_prd} using R-inla to get the posterior predictive
> mean and sd of the {y_prd}.
> But I want to know what is the posterior predictive distribution of
> {y_prd | y_obs}? Since Gaussian likelihood is used, is that also
> Gaussian or at least can be approximated by a Gaussian? If so, what is
> the mean (posterior mean) and covariance structure?

you cannot get y_prd in INLA directly. what you get is the posterior for
the linear predictor and you can from this compute the posterior for
y_prd.

as the gaussian response have (likely) an unknown precision and to do
that correct, I would use inla.posterior.sample() to generate (iid)
samples from the posterior and from this sample y_prd. this is the easy
solution...

it all depends on how involved you want to make it

let me know if this is still unclear.

H


--

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Basic question about the posterior distribution
parts:
Hi,

In the full Bayesian analysis, the marginal posterior distribution at a location isn't actually Gaussian, and inla instead computes it as a mixture of Gaussians.  Sampling from the posterior can then be used for full posterior predictions.

If you instead do an "empirical Bayes" analysis (strategy="eb"), _then_ the posterior distributions are Gaussian, like you discuss.  In this case, adding the squared prediction sd and the estimated observation variance will give the data prediction variance.

Finn L

messages.author: afb003e064114795
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Basic question about the posterior distribution
parts:
On 22 Aug 2014, at 16:19, ming li <ming.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
Hey, thanks! I wonder if you mean marginal prediction/variance? Since the prediction y_prd = (y_1,...,y_n) is a vector and can I get the predictive covariance of it rather than only marignal variance?

The usual output only gives you the marginal distribution properties for each y.
For values obtained using the "lincomb" feature you can also get the joint covariance matrix (if n is small enough to actually store the matrix).
Otherwise you need to use sampling; inla.posterior.sample can be used to sample from the joint posterior.

Finn L
